subsubtopic: SUGGESTED ACTION TO CREATE BETTER RELATIONS BETWEEN UNION AND MANAGEMENT-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. Because of the continuing malaise in labour-management relations inside ,the Post Office-a phrase often used by the former postmaster general-a malaise which has now degenerated into impasse according to the new Postmaster General in his speech to the Canadian Postal Users' Conference this week, management having broken the spirit of the December, 1975 collective agreement with the Canadian Union of Postal Workers by failing to inform the union executive about new equipment being installed in St. John's Newfoundland, and London, Ontario, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Churchill (Mr. Smith):
That the Postmaster General take immediate steps to make management less autocratic, thereby lessening the need of the union to coerce, and as an essential step, to restoring with CUPW an atmosphere of mutual confidence and trust similar to that which has been established with the letter carriers union over recent months, thus assuring the people of Canada the quality of postal service they formerly enjoyed and have every right to expect.

subsubtopic: RESULTS OF DISCUSSIONS WITH FRANCE ON EXTENSION BY CANADA OF FISHING ZONE TO TWO HUNDRED MILES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct my question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The minister has recently returned from France and I should like to ask him this question. In light of the important social and economic impact of the fisheries on the people of Atlantic Canada, may I ask the minister whether agreement has been reached between Canada and France over the conflict of interest between our two countries with regard to the extension of our fishing limit to 200 miles, bearing in mind that while he was attending to his duties in Paris his counterpart, the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment, made an announcement in this House and served statutory notice of his intention to declare a 200 mile limit effective January 1, 1977?

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: RESULTS OF DISCUSSIONS WITH FRANCE ON EXTENSION BY CANADA OF FISHING ZONE TO TWO HUNDRED MILES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to give the hon. member and the House as much information as I can today. I undertake as well to have a statement prepared over the weekend
November 5, 1976

regarding the Canada-France negotiations; there simply has not been time for me to put it together. On the matter of the St. Pierre and Miquelon-Canada situation, we held discussions lately at the ministerial level in Paris which were a follow on of discussions which have been underway between officials for sometime. It is evident that it will not be possible, as it was not possible with the United States, to conclude and finalize all aspects of this question before January 1.
However, in a most amiable discussion and negotiation, France and Canada undertook to put in place an interim agreement or arrangement, which will be done before January 1; the mutual objective, as stated by each side during the talks in Paris, is to prevent any disruption or serious change in the situation as of January 1. In the meantime long-term discussions will continue and the interim arrangement will eventually be replaced with what 1 am satisfied will be a mutually agreeable solution.

speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. I thank the minister for his reply and appreciate that he recently returned and has not had time to prepare a report. 1 hope that when it is ready the report will be presented to the House and not outside the House, so that we will have the opportunity to examine it. My supplementary question is as follows: Since there has obviously been a lack of agreement to date on this important matter, I should like to know if there was any discussion of quotas which would be allocated to France under the 1CNAF arrangement covering zones three and four; also, have any special arrangements been made between Canada and France in this particular area?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DISCUSSIONS WITH FRANCE ON ALLOCATION OF FISHING QUOTAS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first, I assure the hon. member that, on the matter of providing full information, I will be pleased to consult with him and other interested members on the best means for giving detailed information to the House; we could perhaps do that after the weekend. One is the ICNAF quota arrangements for 1977 which will form the basis for setting up quotas in the zones to which the hon. member referred. Of course, there is in addition a 1972 treaty between Canada and France which is not affected substantively by the announcement of the 200-mile zone extension made by my colleague on my behalf and his own two days ago.

Mr. Speaker, the many issues to which the hon. member referred have not been settled finally. 1 believe 1 indicated prior to the declaration made two days ago that action was being taken without prejudice and that negotiations with the United States would continue. Canada has drawn what is properly described by the hon. member as an equidistant line which goes through Georges Bank. The United States in response, and incidentally in consultation, for we were aware it was going to be done, has drawn a different line with which I am sure the hon. member is familiar. Each of these actions has been taken without prejudice. subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
moved that Bill C-19, to amend or repeal certain statutes to enable restraint of government expenditures, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in opening the debate on second reading of the bill, which is not a lengthy bill but a very significant one, I want to take the opportunity of paying tribute to my predecessor, who has now taken over the responsibilities of trade and commerce, for his performance and effectiveness during his regime in this portfolio, particularly in the area of expenditure restraint. This bill is important to that effort, of course.
As I move into a greater awareness of my responsibilities as President of the Treasury Board, I am beginning to realize fully the extraordinary competence with which my predecessor addressed the problems that he faced and which I now inherit. I shall continue to try to perform in the manner he did. I know that the shoes are big to fill, and 1 realize, based upon my experience as a "line-operating departmental minister", the difficulties of having to deal with one's colleagues and all sorts of meritorious suggestions for the improvement of government programs, policy and services, all of which, of course, also carry with them a dollar figure. The success of my predecessor has, I think, already been apparent and will be more apparent when the full fiscal framework story of 1976-77 is written. Indeed, I can confirm now that he will have been able during his period of the fiscal year to meet his commitments on the kind of restraint figures that he announced in this House.
One of the government measures required to complete that story is passage of Bill C-19. Last December 18, as one of the many steps the government was taking to bring inflation under control, certain reductions in planned government expenditures for the fiscal year 1976-77 were announced. These reductions were categorized as deferrals of planned expenditures, elimina-

November 5, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
tion of planned expenditures and elimination of activities. I should like to give some examples of reductions in expenditures. As the House knows, we moved to freeze the salaries of the members of this House, members of the other House, of all judges of the Supreme Court, judges in the Federal Court and provincial superior courts, as well as public servants in the higher-salaried categories. We shall also terminate the program known as Opportunities for Youth and the agencies known as Information Canada and the Company of Young Canadians. This bill contains authority to eliminate in the year 1976 the indexation of family allowances, and also to defer or reduce loans to Crown corporations or require them to obtain their funds from the commercial sector.
The total reduction in planned expenditures for these and many other items was about $1.5 billion, of which slightly more than half is reductions in budgetary expenditures, the remainder being reductions in non-budgetary expenditures. Had these reductions not been imposed, the main estimates which were tabled in the House on February 18, 1976, would have been about $1 billion higher than they were and the capital budgets of Crown corporations, which are approved by orders in council and also tabled in this House, would have been about $500 million higher. The levels of expenditure for some of the items involved in these reductions are regulated by specific provisions in certain acts of parliament. Of course, to effect the reductions it is necessary to amend those provisions.
Hon. members will recall that this bill was first introduced-that is, given first reading-last March, but was not proceeded with prior to the summer recess, or the end of the previous session. Consequently, the bill, with minor revisions, was given first reading again a few days ago, on November 1. The revisions relate to the effective dates for certain amendments. The purpose of the omnibus legislation now before hon. members is to provide the authority necessary for enabling certain planned expenditure reductions to be made. I will try to itemize the intent and major provisions of the bill, although I think most of them are familiar to hon. members.
The bill would amend the Adult Occupational Training Act. Sections 7 and 8 of the act are being repealed and new sections substituted. This change is necessary to eliminate the present statutory requirement for an automatic annual escalation of trainee allowances which have been based, and are still based, on increases in the manufacturing wage index, and to substitute a provision which would permit the setting of these allowances by regulation, without reference to an indexing provision, subsequent to an annual review by the minister. This would come after reference of the matter to cabinet. Under the present act, training allowances are increased annually on July 1 in accordance with the increase in the manufacturing wage index for the previous calendar year.
Another clause of the act deals with the Company of Young Canadians. The Company of Young Canadians Act is to be repealed, and the provisions of the bill provide for the transfer of the Company's assets and liabilities to Her Majesty and for

the Secretary of State to administer the closing out of the Company.
The Family Allowances Act, 1973, is to be amended. New subsections are being added to that act so that for 1976 the rates at which the allowance will be paid will be frozen at the 1975 level. It will be made clear that provincial rates for family allowances may be specified by provincial regulations. Other amendments are consequential to those measures, of course. Indeed, as some hon. members noted in the throne speech debate, the indexation of family allowances is planned to begin again on January 1,1977.
The bill will repeal the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act. However, before that can be accomplished the act must be amended in order to end the period during which assistance is available for the support of the costs of conducting research and development and to provide that all applications for grants will be cut off as of December 31, 1976. The amendments provide that once the provisions of the act are fulfilled, it may be repealed by proclamation of the governor in council.
The bill also deals with Appropriation Act No. 3, 1970, vote 25 of Supply and Services. This vote was the legislation which set up Information Canada and the vote must be repealed so that Information Canada may be formally abolished. The bill also amends the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Section 41 of the act is being amended so as to authorize my colleague, the Minister of Finance, to postpone crediting amounts in the consolidated revenue fund to the stabilization account until a later date, at which time interest would also be credited.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill as revised by the government has finally been presented to
November 5, 1976

the House. It was announced earlier last year. Since then there has been a change of minister and we now have a new President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). The previous bill was a famous non-starter, although it was on the government's list of priorities for action prior to the summer recess. The previous bill was Bill C-87 which, if one ignores some differences in the last clause as to applicability, is essentially the same as the bill now before the House.
As the President of the Treasury Board mentioned, many aspects of a special nature will be dealt with by other ministers. Similarly, many of my colleagues have a special interest in particular clauses. Clause 14 has to do with grain stabilization; other parts of the bill deal with adult training, family allowances, etc. 1 am primarily concerned with the over-view of government spending and want to put in proper perspective this so-called restraint. Is this restraint? Is it cutting back? Is this cosmetic, or is it merely transferring expenditures from one account to another?
1 am thinking of the cutting down of the adult training program. The result will be a greater drop-out rate among student trainees who will then have to go on unemployment insurance or social assistance. From the standpoint of the Canadian public, this is just a reshuffling of cards. There is no reduction in public spending resulting from restraint. We are told there is going to be a reduction of $20 million or so in the capital budget brought about by the elimination of cost of living escalations which are tied in with certain wage rate increases. The net result is that trainees who are at the real subsistence level will find, because of the change in the legislation, that they cannot make it, and will drop out. Then where do they go?
The program was designed to take them off the unemployment rolls. Instead, we will be paying them unemployment insurance, if they qualify, and if they do not qualify they will, unfortunately, have to resort to some sort of social assistance. Now there are more who will drop out and will resort to those two avenues of assistance, their only sources, in order to keep body and soul together. What is not realized, and what should be explained by the government, is that there is this coldly calculated treatment in dealing with people who are in trouble and are merely being shifted through another door. This is not dealing with the problem. It is not a restraint program in any way. It is merely a matter of shunting something to somewhere else where it can be lost. Nothing is being said about reducing payments to the Unemployment Insurance Commission in so far as the federal deficit is concerned.
When we look at the billions of dollars of federal government subsidies to the Unemployment Insurance Commission, one could say there is almost another $20 million which can be lost in those billions. That is precisely what is happening. What 1 would really like the minister to propose in this particular sector is improvement in long-term planning. The average vacancy rate, representing an actual loss to the manpower retraining scheme, has been in the nature of 17 per cent.
Restraint of Government Expenditures In other words, the government of Canada, through its Manpower division, contracts for so much training time either with provincial institutions or others: there is a commitment which has to be met.
On the basis of 1973-74, the vacancy rate for the annual occupational training program was 17.1 per cent. The vacancy rate has not been reduced in the past few years. A vacancy rate of approximately 17 per cent indicates that the government is wasting in the order of $63 million in training time, as well as a comparable amount in training allowances. By an increase in the rates payable to adults receiving training allowances, the total cost of the program could increase but the net loss may decrease due to more individuals remaining for the duration of the program.
The government will not reduce the Canada Manpower budget unless it dramatically decreases its services to the general public and decreases the number of people receiving Canada Manpower training. The individuals now receiving Canada Manpower training require the upgrading allowed under this program, and any reduction in this portion of the Canada Manpower budget will lead to too many unnecessary hardships to individuals who can least afford it. As I pointed out, their only alternative will be to resort to unemployment insurance if they are qualified, and if not qualified, to fall back on social assistance.
The provinces are paying half the social assistance and the government of Canada is paying the other half. It is the little man, the Canadian taxpayer, who wants to see restraint or reduction in government spending programs, because he is the man standing there now with his pockets wide open and empty. Why? I should like to quote from a very authoritative publication, one to which I have resorted on many occasions, National Finances, which is compiled annually by the Canadian Tax Foundation. I will point out the change that has occurred in the past decade, taking into account inflation, the increase in population and the increase in economic activity. Table 2-8, which appears at page 15 of the 1975-76 issue of National Finances, indicates that in the decade 1965 to 1974, inclusive, the share of total government revenue, expressed in percentage of gross national product, went from 30.3 per cent to 40.4 per cent.
We do not yet have the figures for 1975, but the public sector-that is, the productive sector of the country-says that the share of the gross national product which has gone to governments, municipal, provincial and federal, in either direct or indirect taxes has increased by one-third in a decade. We started out with 30.3 per cent, and finished with 40.4 per cent, an increase of 10 percentage points in GNP. Over a decade, that means an increase of one-third. That is part of the problem in Canada. That is part of the problem of inflation contributed to by the federal government of Canada. Many factors lead to inflation, but government unrestrained spending is one of the most serious ones.
806

November 5, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures
In the past decade we saw the pile of resources produced by Canadians, goods and services which have become available to the public sector to spend, go up by one-third. Now we have to sit back and examine the totality of these programs. It is something that we can expect to see in the next ten years. If that rate of expansion of public expenditure continues, we will remember the rate of increase of public expenditure, of GNP, will have been 33 per cent, or one-third, in the past decade. Let us assume that that rate of increase in expenditures continues over the next decade-and there is nothing to suggest that it will go down-then I suggest the word "restraint" may not be applicable. If we go a further third in government spending, we will see that by 1984, eight years from now, almost 54 per cent of the Canadian GNP will fall into the realm of public expenditure.
I am dealing with the rate of increase. If it goes over from one decade to the next without a reduction-in other words, if no restraint is applied-then I suggest that is a possible perimeter of the level of the GNP which the government will take. I strongly assert, and I think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) would agree with me, that that would create problems in this country, particularly on the question of investment of capital in productive resources and the rate of return on invested capital which is the greatest stimulant to further investment. For either the renewal of productive resources or the development of further productive resources this would create problems.
Let us consider how the government of Canada will spend its money in 1976 and how its expenditures are projected for 1977, because we now have the estimates before us. I will ask leave, when I complete my remarks, for this table which is compiled from the estimates and the supplementary estimates to form part of the record of today's proceedings. The table was compiled by the Canadian Tax Foundation and I accept responsibility for it. I can table it or read it in its entirety. I ask leave to table it as an appendix to today's Hansard, Mr. Speaker.

I thank hon. members for their consideration; it will make examination of the program that much simpler. The 1976 estimates provided that interest on the public debt be $3,930 million, or 11.3 per cent of federal expenditures. However, in 1977 interest on the public debt will have gone up by $720 million to a total of $4,650 million, or 12.1 per cent of total government expenditures. Under the heading of National Health and Welfare there is to be-this includes old age security, GIS, spouse's allowance, the Canada Assistance Plan, hospital insurance, medicare, family allowances, the health resources fund, and miscellane-

ous-an expenditure of $9,886.7 million, or 28.5 per cent of the federal expenditures. In 1977 that total will have gone up to $10,881 million, or 28.3 per cent. However, the government of Canada's contribution to the unemployment insurance fund in 1976 is estimated to be $890 million, or 2.6 per cent, but- and this may startle hon. members-the government examines all its factors and says that for 1977 it expects that contribution to be $1,700 million, almost double what it was in 1976, for 4.4 per cent of total government expenditures to meet the deficit in unemployment insurance.
I do not have to go through all the other figures, such as figures for national defence, which are more or less static, unconditional transfers to provinces, which are more or less static; oil compensation payments, with a gentle lowering; manpower training and service allowances, which are static; payments for post-secondary education, which are being frozen and are therefore static; and the bilingualism program, which is also relatively static. The Figures for transport are static, including air, water, railways and roads, and others; public works and programs, which is a very small item; and the Post Office, which is going from $896.5 million, or 2.6 per cent, to $1,122 million or 2.9 per cent; Indian Affairs and Northern Development-this is a strange priority-remains static; and agriculture and grains go down.

They go down from $957 million to $862 million. Under miscellaneous there is an increase of $600 million, but the percentage is about the same. The total budgetary expenditure at the federal level for 1976 will be just $34,691 billion. In 1977 it is estimated to be $38,417 billion. We here cannot answer for, control or influence the level of provincial expenditures, but if we are talking about restraint in spending programs and the philosophy of government spending programs over-all, I want to reassert what 1 said earlier about the percentage of gross national product which goes into the public sector: it is a frightening picture. It could be that some of our colleagues in the New Democratic Party will say that it is a glorious picture for them, but the public sector is not producing that GNP.
I want to discuss an area in which we have to re-examine levels of expenditure. The provinces have a clear ride in this area and there is no accountability to the money market. They have accountability to their legislatures for their spending programs, but the money market is something which says where you can get your money. The provinces have the ability to go to the Canada Pension fund and to borrow right up to their level of contributions less a proportion for administrative expenses, but then we see that they are not paying interest. They are supposed to be paying some interest in cash to the Canada Pension fund, but they are not. There is no transfer back from the provinces, though they would have to do so if they were floating bonds on the market among their citizens.
November 5, 1976

Restraint of Government Expenditures

They have been permitted to capitalize their interest payments to the Canada Pension fund; in other words, issue more provincial bonds. That will be all right until 1982, when the cash contributions from the John and Jane Citizens of this country will not cover the payout and there will have to be some realization of assets of the fund in order to cover the payout. There is a day of reckoning, but 1 suggest that no provincial administration, under this system, feels any restraint because it knows that its citizens are taxed in an indirect way under the guise of the Canada Pension Plan and governments make no contribution to the fund other than as employers.
This money, then, is taken out of the hands of the citizens of a province and sequestered into a fund which is immediately turned over to the province, and that is a source of income. I suggest that instead of starting from square one in finance, the responsibilities of the provinces start from square ten because there is no accountability to anyone with regard to that money, particularly not the money market. If a province had to justify expenditures against its revenue capabilities, the money market would soon tell the provincial treasurers and cabinets where they were overspending. This is very serious and we will have to deal with it. Is the government of Canada and the governments of the provinces serious about their restraint programs, or are they merely shuffling cards?
My colleagues will examine this program, as laid out in Bill C-19, in great detail. I suggest that there is not very much in the bill as far as restraint is concerned. As I said, a good deal of what is contained in the bill is a matter of shuffling cards from one program into another program which is not very readily identifiable. We will examine this bill in detail. I think there will be a long debate on this bill. It merits close attention, although individually the items themselves have not very much import, with the possible exception of clauses 14 and 15. After all, stabilization is merely a postponement of payments; the payments will still have to be made. This bill requires very careful attention. We should be able to analyse the real intent of the government with regard to its restraint on the rim of public expenditure, and 1 suggest that we must come to grips with the rate of increase of public expenditure.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 shall not detain the House much longer, having made most of my remarks. I wish to draw the attention of hon. members and the public at large, however, to one of the areas in which 1 feel the government has been extraordinarily shortsighted with regard to the application of this so-called restraint program.
Prior to one o'clock 1 spent a good deal of my time indicating just how large a chunk of the gross national product the government of Canada was taking. We have seen reports almost ad nauseam in number and in content about the difficulties Canadian industry, Canadian trade and, in fact, the whole Canadian economy is facing at the present time with regard to reduced productivity, our difficulties in selling abroad, our fantastically high wage rates compared to our competitors, and our extraordinarily high unit costs.
When you come down to it-and I do not care whether it is a raw product, a basic resource material, semi-processed, or the most sophisticated piece of machinery equipment or consumer goods-if the price that has to be paid for the continuing production of the commodity is too high for the market.
80001 -S2'/2

November 5, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures then that is the end of the road. In so many commodities today we have reached the end of the road unless we mend our ways. What are the areas in which Canadian industry, Canadian labour and Canadian government can participate jointly, freely and with enlightened self-interest in each sector? Is it the encouragement and the development of Canadian industrial research? We cannot stand still, Mr. Speaker. What do we see in this bill, however? What is the area in which restraint should be applied? Is it a total wind-down of government assistance in this particular form to industrial development and research?
I suppose that from the bureaucratic point of view there is something to commend this type of close-down. We know all too well that in the insular shell of government administration there is one principle that applies with agonizing repetitiveness. That is, "Not invented here". In other words, we did not think about it, we did not work on it, we did not develop it, and therefore it is no good and should not be allowed. It is a human trait, I suppose, but "Not invented here" or "NIH" has a terrible influence within government administrative circles. The burden is on the minister to indicate that the cost benefit usefulness of this program is wound down; that it is completely taken out of circulation as of December 31 this year. To that extent I put the minister to the proof and I suggest it will likely be the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) who has responsibility for this program.
I do not think the government has made its case with regard to imposing restraint, certainly not restraint in the way I spelled it out. There has been imposed on the government, by its self-discipline, the principle that the rate of increase in the gross national product that is being taken by the government shall be reduced. 1 have said, and I am sure my colleagues will point it out even more clearly, that this program is just a shuffling of cards. Certain programs that may have a certain identity are cut out and then shuffled to unemployment insurance or here or there. To that extent, the burden of proof is on the President of the Treasury Board and his colleagues. The ministers will defend the particular points put forward in this bill. It is certainly not incumbent upon the opposition to prove that the government is wrong in putting forward the bill in this particular form.
I invite my colleagues and other members of the House to participate in this debate because it goes to the fundamental basis of what this country is going to do in the next ten years.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO REMOVE CERTAIN RESTRICTIONS RESPECTING TRAINING ALLOWANCE RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in many ways Bill C-19, restraint of government expenditures, should be subtitled "a Tory conversion bill". It contains a whole package of measures for which the Progressive Conservative party has been asking a long time. It shows the kind of trouble that Liberal governments get themselves into when they do not have the NDP around to kick them in the shins once in a while. As long as we were around and they were in a minority position, we could kick them in a progressive direction. However, the terrible misfortune of a majority govern-
[Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West).)
ment befell them in the last election. Therefore, they do not have anyone to straighten them out from time to time and they tend to respond to the blandishments of the Progressive Conservative party in their posture of restraint. It would not be so bad if my friends to the right were grateful, but they are not. They are not showering the government with any laurels for this bill. I think of one item in particular.
During the last campaign, the Conservative platform was strongly loaded in the direction of cutting back government expenditures. We asked the Conservative candidates what kind of government expenditures they would cut out. We asked whether they would cut out family allowances or old age pensions. To their credit, they were in favour of family allowances and old age pensions. As it turned out, the only thing they would only cut out was Information Canada. Information Canada was the great villain of the last election campaign. The government has cut out Information Canada in this bill. As I say, I see no gratitude on the part of my friends on the right. As a matter of fact, when the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) spoke, he did not even have the courtesy of mentioning that Information Canada was one of the items being cut out.
Hon. friends to my right are all for getting rid of government programs. They say they want to get rid of useless government programs, not the good ones. However, it is always difficult to determine what they consider useful and what they consider useless. Let me give one example that was framed by the hon. member for Edmonton West in his address to this House. He seems to regret that the Industrial Research and Development Incentives Act is being cut out, despite the fact it is not being cut out because the government is trying to save money. My understanding is that they have not been able to give away any money under that act, so they might as well get rid of it. Our position would be that if you cannot encourage industrial development or industrial research with those kinds of provisions, you encourage it under some other provision. We are not going to fight in favour of keeping an item for which there is obviously no earthly use.
I listened very carefully, in the hope that I would get some advance support on a very important item that is being cut out. Of all things the government chooses to cut out in a year when people in Canada are experiencing great difficulty, they pick on family allowances. This is the great beast to which the government is going to apply the axe. I had hoped that some word in defence of the indexing of family allowances would have come from my friends to the right. After all, they were in favour of indexing. They wanted to index the Income Tax Act. Not only did they want to, but they were so successful that they persuaded the government to act in a Tory way and index the Income Tax Act, in spite of the knowledge that indexing income tax is of infinitely greater benefit to those who have a lot of money than to those who have not. They are in favour of indexing the Income Tax Act, removing hundreds of millions of dollars from the government. The way in which that loss of revenue will be made up is by depriving people who receive family allowances of the benefits of indexing.
November 5, 1976

That is a very nice trade-off, obviously one which we in this party cannot possibly agree with. However, in the criticism of this bill by my friends to the right, there was not a single word about what the government is doing with family allowances. That is particularly criminal with a measure of this kind, considering an ad that appeared in a morning newspaper placed by the Citizens' Coalition. It is a horrible ad and 1 do not agree with the conclusions, but there is an element of truth in it. The ad set out to attack the indexing of public service pensions. That was the whole purpose of the advertisement-to attack the idea of indexing civil servants' pensions, despite the fact that the indexing provision is part of the total passage on the basis of which salaries are negotiated.
What will make it difficult for this government or any other government to justify the indexing of civil servants' pensions is the fact that a decision has been taken to remove the indexing provision as it applies to family allowances. Before this decision was made we pointed out, when this question of the indexing of civil servants' pensions was raised, that old age pensions were indexed, that parliamentary allowances were indexed and that income tax allowances were indexed. We were able to point out that a broad range of people benefited from indexing, not just civil servants.
But what has happened now? The government has an instinct for self-destruction which is almost impossible to credit. It is in serious trouble now, yet it goes to great pains to make matters even worse. At a time when members of parliament are under attack for the indexing of their pensions, the government does away with the indexing of family allowances. Who benefits, in the main, from family allowances? It is true that some of them go to well-off people, but it is the poor, with large families, who benefit most substantially. We retain the principle of escalation as it applies to members of parliament and public servants, but we remove it in the case of people in receipt of family allowances. Aside from the unconscionable nature of an act of this kind, its stupidity cannot be overlooked. Yet not one word has been said by hon. members to my right condemning this effrontery toward recipients of family allowances, or criticizing the government because these people have been singled out to bear the brunt of the cuts the government believes to be necessary during a period of restraint.
I listened to what was said by the hon. member for Edmonton West about the way in which government expenditures are increasing. In fairness to him, the federal government, whose share of the gross national product has increased, if I remember the figures he used correctly, from 30.3 per cent ten years ago to 40.4 per cent today, was not his only target. He deplored that increase. I wonder what the comparable figures for the hon. member's native province of Alberta would be, because in that province the increase in government revenues has been phenomenal. Who is paying this lax which accrues to the coffers of Alberta? Other Canadians. 1 am not implying that Alberta is being unfair; the province is not charging the world price. We have been able to persuade Alberta, by one
Restraint of Government Expenditures means or another, to keep its price below the world price. But be realistic. What we are seeing here is a transfer of income from one group of Canadians to another.
Would the hon. member propose that this accidental increase in the price of oil, this increase which has nothing to do with the skill or intelligence of the oil companies, should all go to the credit of those companies? His figures would then look somewhat better, and instead of saying that over the last ten years the federal share of the GNP had increased from 30 per cent to rather more than 40 per cent, he would be quoting a final figure of, say, 38 per cent because the other 2 per cent had gone into the pockets of the oil companies. I make these comments to illustrate how ridiculous it is to use figures of this kind when comparing the proportion of the gross national product taken by the public sector as against the private sector, without directing attention to the use being made of these moneys.
If, for example, the share taken by the private sector was unusually large and it was being used for frivolous purposes, would that have been satisfactory? If the share taken by the public sector was used, as it is used, in supplying hospitals, education, medical services, and so on, is that bad; or if it is used to make oil compensation payments for the benefit of people who live in one part of Canada as opposed to another. I am sure the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Stanfield)-who I see in his place-is concerned about the difficulty in which oil consumers in his province now find themselves and what would be likely to happen if those compensation payments were reduced or removed as the government is threatening.
Is the expenditure we are talking about so terrible, or is it merely a reflection of the fact that we are living in a society which has become somewhat more sensitive to the needs of particular groups of Canadians, to the need for sharing? As the percentage of government expenditure increases by comparison with private expenditures, what really happens is this: a redistribution of income is taking place in a manner different from the way in which redistribution is brought about in the marketplace. Most people, I believe, would agree that the redistribution which takes place through the government sector is considerably fairer and, very often, more useful and more humane than the other approach.
There is a perverse logic to Bill C-19. It is difficult for me to look at the title without feeling anger. The title is "Restraint of government expenditures". The reverse logic is that there are a number of government programs involving both expenditure and taxation which have proven to be both costly and ineffective. Yet there is not a word in the bill about the cancellation of those programs.
Let me refer to the accelerated depreciation allowances which are now part of the Income Tax Act, or to the provisions for the reduction of corporation taxes which are now part of that act. When these measures were introduced, we were told they would increase employment opportunities. That was the argument advanced in justification of those measures. While this meant that personal income tax payers would have to assume a heavier share of the burden of being citizens of

November 5, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures Canada, that was the reason given. What are the facts? What does the record show? Almost from the day these measures were brought in, unemployment in Canada has been increasing, until today the unemployment figure has reached almost 700,000, the highest since the great depression. Where are all these give-away programs, these billions of dollars in forgone revenue designed by the government to create employment? Despite these programs, investment is at a new low. The companies who received these benefits were asked to comment and state the extent to which they had been able to increase employment as a result. The answer was that it was negligible: employment was not increasing as a result of these benefits.
If you want to exercise restraint, Mr. Speaker, you should look at programs that have proven to be ineffective, and cut them. But no, the government uses a different logic. If you dispensed with indexation of family allowances, this would save the government $230 million a year. Those who have examined the economy of this country have pointed out that one reason Canada has had a less severe recession than the United States is that consumer purchasing power has been maintained. Family allowances and indexed family allowances are part of that purchasing power and have contributed toward saving us from an even worse recession than the one we are now experiencing. This is not true of the example I gave of the corporate tax benefits, yet this is the program that is being cut.
Take another case of perversity. I can understand the government's cutting out Information Canada; it had to make a response. This was the great bete noire of the Progressive Conservative party, and since it is now government policy to try to outdo the Tories and be more Tory than the Tories, it had to get rid of Information Canada. It is not that anyone really believes that this will do much good, or that this is a real cut, or that the expenditures made on Information Canada will not be made in some other department or area, or that some other functions that were performed by Information Canada will not be performed in some other area.
Let me go to one other item, the Company of Young Canadians. This is being cut. I know it has been a very controversial body, but it was designed to be controversial. When the CYC was set up, it was designed to be a troublemaking organization; it was designed to be anti-establishment; it was designed to stimulate activity. You cannot do this without making some mistakes.

speechtext:
They cannot say it's peanuts any more, either, because that would be a sort of international insult. It is getting tougher and tougher, Mr. Speaker, to make a speech with all these limitations being placed on a person. The Company of Young Canadians did, I think, a remarkable job with that kind of budget. Their budget was pared from the previous year's budget of $5.9 million in 1975-76, which was a little more than the budget of 1974 and 1973. They employed persons of an age and category who represented the most difficult challenge to employment. Among the young people of Canada the rate of unemployment is at least twice as high as that of other groups.
To what extent, Mr. Speaker, is this going to be a real saving? We are cutting out $3.7 million, or $5.9 million, depending on which year's budget you are looking at. But how much will be a real saving? These kids were operating at barely above minimum wage, and considering some of the hours they were putting in, they did not even get minimum wage. It is not as if there is alternate employment for them. If we had an economy that was fully employed, or if we had a tremendous labour shortage, we could well say that this was a direct saving because these people could work somewhere else and thus save the federal budget money. But this is not going to happen, Mr. Speaker. There are far less than 100,000 jobs available for the 700,000 people who are unemployed, so at the very best, using outside figures, the prospects of a young man of this sort finding employment are 1 in 14. Even though 1 in 14 may find employment, the others will have to be sustained, probably by unemployment insurance or some other kind of support program. So what is saved by this kind of magnificent gesture? However, what is lost, Mr. Speaker, is significant. What is lost is a group of young idealists who did an effective job. It was not a job with which 1 always agreed. As a matter of fact, on many occasions I was critical of some of the work they did. Nevertheless it was one of the most idealistic and activist groups that we had in this country. We could not stand it; we had to kill it off in the name of budgetary restraint-1 suggest a false name indeed.
Although some of the cuts in the bill had to be made because the funds were not being used effectively, the CYC was effective. It was not costing us a great deal of money. Nevertheless, the government had to put a package together; it had to show it could out-Tory the Tories on this, and this is the result.
To look upon a bill like this as some kind of solution, or even a part solution-I know the government is not claiming that it is the only solution-to the problems afflicting our society is a disgrace. Although these cuts are being made, the Minister of
November 5, 1976

Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Cullen) is going to bring in the son of EIP, or the son of OFY, or perhaps even the son of CYC. The government are going to bring in another range of programs that perhaps will work under a different minister.
The Minister of Manpower and Immigration speaks of enlarging the job opportunities program. How many jobs are going to be created? Not very many. I am not going to knock the program because it does not create that many jobs. If it creates any jobs at all, it is worth while, especially with as many unemployed as we have in Canada. But what we on this side of the House fail to see is any real effort on the part of the government to tackle an unemployment level in this country that is disgraceful.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke in Montreal, I think the day before yesterday, and a report appeared in yesterday's Toronto Star headlined "People are not satisfied- and they're right: PM". The report goes on:
Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau last night pleaded with Canadians to learn once again to trust government-despite its bungling.
Trudeau told more than 1.300 businessmen at the annual convention in Montreal of the Federation of Automobile Dealer Associations that "before we can even begin to solve the problem of your business and our laws, we have to solve a much more basic problem-the understanding between government and the people.
"People are not satisfied, and God knows they have cause not to be satisfied in our country-the way we've bungled things.
1 do not condemn such public soul-searching, but there is reason for the present lack of confidence. The Prime Minister's admitting that the government has bumbled is no disgrace. From time to time all governments bumble. But not meaning what he says, that is the disgrace. If the Prime Minister means what he says, if he has really concluded that the government is not performing as it should, we should see evidence of his concern. But there is no such indication. We only see a tendency on the part of the government to run scared to death of polls which show the Progressive Conservative party rising in the public esteem. When this happens, the Liberals traditionally say, "Let's look for someone else's clothes on the clothes' line. We don't like the NDP clothes; let's try on the Tory pants." Unfortunately, such clothes, such ideas, do not fit the Liberals very well; they do not fit the Tories well, either. That is the bumbling Liberal way for solving these dilemmas and, not surprisingly, the situation remains a shambles. The government still does not know how to curtail unemployment.

speechtext:
If the Prime Minister is sincere in what he says about this government's bungling and wants to change things, he must act positively. Incidentally, 1 should like to address my remarks particularly to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration who is present in the chamber and has said some of the things I am about to say. If we are worried about our future, we must be concerned about the present. We know that in the long run unemployment will go away, but I do not like to join John Keynes in what he says about the long run.
Restraint of Government Expenditures
We need to solve this country's unemployment difficulties soon. At present there is unemployment, and some time in the future we shall face a labour shortage. Surely the government will not wait to act until that future shortage develops. If it waits, it will encounter problems as severe as those it faces today. It seems to me, since fewer young people will be available in the society of the future to do our work, they will need to be exceedingly productive if they are to provide for themselves and those who are retired and are no longer in the work force a decent standard of living.
What am I saying, Mr. Speaker? We must do our best to curtail present unemployment. Many things in this country need to be done, and if we want to ensure a satisfactory future for our society they should be done. For example, factories need to be improved, railways need to be built, we need more storage facilities for grain in order to avoid present boom and bust cycles. We must create the infrastructure which will be needed in the future, and by so doing allow those who want to work the opportunity of working.
I say all this because the costs of unemployment are horrendous, in human as well as economic terms. Last year by reason of unemployment we lost more than $6 billion worth of goods and services. Tax revenues have been curtailed. In addition to individual contributions to the unemployment insurance fund of about $2 billion, the government itself had to spend $1.7 billion on the program. As well, the government paid about $2.3 billion for family support and welfare programs. This being so, I cannot understand why the government thinks it is cheaper not to be involved in public projects. Why is it on this kick of cutting government expenses? The inevitable result will be horrible losses in the gross national product or, putting it another way, a decline in the output of goods and services.
Apparently the government is cutting expenses for the cosmetic effect. The government is bowing to Conservative pressure. That will be the perceived reason for its action. Certainly, it cannot be defended in logic. The government will be seen as waffling back and forth. People will say that it is not sticking to traditional Liberal party programs; it is trying to be a shadow Conservative party. Therefore people will say, "If the Liberals want to be shadow Tories, we might as well move to the genuine article and vote Tory. We might as well have the real thing."

No, the party does not have very far to go. They have gone in that direction. The government must realize that if the society of the future is to be productive, we cannot afford to waste present-day resources. We cannot tolerate high levels of unemployment, and the government's failure to prepare for the future is, in my view, truly disgraceful. In conclusion, I fail to see the logic behind this bill. Since the government had the chance to evaluate the economy this past summer, it must have seen that conditions are becoming worse in fields of employment. Therefore, to maintain purchasing power it could have changed its mind on eliminating the

Restraint of Government Expenditures indexation of family allowances. As it is, members of parliament whose pensions will be indexed will find it difficult, if not impossible, to justify the government's decision not to index family allowances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) said earlier that the government would cut expenditures by $1 billion in one area and by about $500,000 in another, it is difficult to believe, if one reads this bill, that the reduction in federal expenditures will actually be so great. The government is merely postponing expenditures. There is the suggestion that the 4 per cent federal share of the stabilization fund will not be paid in until it is needed. That makes a mockery of the federal government's previous assurance to farmers that the money would be there. Few farmers will have much confidence in this government.
As mentioned by the previous speaker, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) has urged the people of Canada once more to place their faith and trust in the federal government. How can you do that? In one session of parliament the government said that it would invest an amount equal to 4 per cent of gross sales in the stabilization fund and asked farmers to invest 2 per cent: it said, "We will double the amount you invest." Then in the very next session the government brought in a piece of legislation which stated that it would not put that 4 per cent into the stabilization fund. But we are to rest assured that it will be a bookkeeping entry and that the interest rate will be figured out on the books, and that if it is necessary to draw on that fund, the government of Canada will find the money somewhere.
Let us assume there is a huge reduction in the sale of grain, or that the price comes down substantially and the fund has to be drawn upon the extent of $1 million or $1.5 million. The government then would be tempted to do some accounting so that it would not have to come up with the money, particularly if it were after an election. If it were just before an election, the government would come up with the money somehow or other. This is the reason for the feeling of uneasiness and distrust which people have. It is to be merely a bookkeeping entry and there will not be any saving of money. It is merely a postponement. But through postponement the trust that the Canadian farmers are being asked to place in the government will be destroyed. The Canadian farmer is reluctant to join the stabilization plan because of the distrust of the federal government which they have had for years. There is ample reason for that distrust.
The bill goes on to deal with the Company of Young Canadians, family allowances and a number of other items. I should like to deal more particularly with the "at and east" rates which are being done away with in this bill, where it is merely stated that section 272 of the Railway Act will be deleted. This was a guarantee to the maritime ports, particularly the flour milling trade, that flour mills would receive a subsidy for export. Bill C-19 repeals section 272 of the Rail-

way Act which provides a subsidy in respect of the export of grain and flour by Atlantic and east coast ports.
The shippers of the grain and flour had the right approach at the time these rates were made statutory. The Canadian Transport Commission ascertains the compensatory rate, and the government pays the difference to the railways. This is, therefore, an indirect subsidy to the shippers of the grain and the millers. Is it necessary? What is happening to Canada's trade in flour? It is all very well for the former speaker to talk about jobs and employment. If we mill the wheat into flour, this creates jobs in this country and I think it is important that we should do this.
The U.S.S.R. has told the Canadian government that we can very well lose the Cuban flour market if we raise the price of flour or change the flour subsidy. What does the Cuban flour market mean to the Canadian milling industry? It takes about 80 per cent of the flour we mill. This is very well known to the government. One wonders why the government would attempt to change it and save money in this regard, when this fact is well known. I suppose some speaker will tell us that the milling trade will be subsidized in some other way.
In the Railway Act the "at and east" rates are a statutory provision given in essence to the maritime and eastern ports. They are there. They are an assurance, a guarantee and a trust. One cannot build up the trust which the Prime Minister was speaking about, when we have a policy whereby a subsidy can be given to the millers in one year and taken away in the next. Here, again, I point out that the trust is being eroded in respect of the prairie farmers who have a grain stabilization fund. The trust is being eroded in respect of not only the eastern ports. One could continue to set out the whole matter. In the current calendar year, Canadian exports of flour to Cuba will probably represent something in the order of 375,000 metric tons. This will go to Cuba under an agreement made in 1963. The Cubans receive the flour and Russia pays for it. The transaction was made in 1963 and has been quite successful for Canada since that time.
Canadian flour, however, is in competition with Common Market flour and United States flour. The European Common Market heavily subsidizes the export of flour to many of the underdeveloped countries. The United States does not subsidize the export of its flour, but it exports a great deal of flour in the form of aid programs such as public law 480. The removal of the "at and east" rates will increase the cost of Canadian flour by $15 to $20 a ton. This will place us in a very disadvantageous position with regard to maintaining the Cuban market.
Russia has told the Canadian government, through the Canadian Wheat Board, that if the price of our flour goes up too high, they will build flour mills in Cuba, buy our wheat and mill the flour themselves. What effect will that have on the situation in this country? It will not help the situation at all. What has happened in recent years in respect of the whole flour industry? The total world trade in flour has remained relatively constant over the past ten years, at something like five billion metric tons.
November 5, 1976

The Canadian share of the world flour market has drastically decreased. Ten years ago Canadian millers received something like 18 per cent of the world flour trade. Today that figure is down to 10 per cent even with the advantage of selling flour to Cuba. One must, of course, look at the whole flour industry to see what has happened. Back in 1956, for example, there were 78 flour mills in Canada, and today there are 39. That give one an idea what really is taking place in the milling industry. We are slowly shrinking in our ability to compete throughout the world because of the subsidies of the European Common Market in respect of the flour milling industry and because of U.S. shipments of flour in the form of aid to underdeveloped countries. Canada is not in a very good competitive position.
We should really reconsider Clause 15 of this bill and perhaps even delete it because it is of no advantage to the country as a whole. It does not save us any money, and the government is destroying a little more of the trust which the people have placed in government in recent years. We must try to build up that trust; we must try to build up markets and create jobs in this country.
As I stated, the volume of trade that is available to Canada as a result of the export of flour paid for by the Russians, shipped to Cuba and then distributed by Cuba as assistance to some of the African countries, has been beneficial to the Canadian grain industry, the Canadian milling industry, and to the Canadian ports. The Canadian Wheat Board has been told by the U.S.S.R. grain buying agency that if flour goes up in price, they will stop buying it from us. The agreement stands only as long as the at and east rates are left alone. 1 know that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) or the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) can rise in the House and assure us and the milling industry, with whom they have had many meetings, that they will be compensated in another way, but in my view this assurance will not be sufficient to ensure the continuity of the milling industry. You cannot modernize plants and improve their milling capacity on the sole guarantee of a year to year subsidy to a particular plant or port. Also, such a subsidy will establish a precedent. People will be asking themselves which ports will receive such a subsidy-will it be available only to the milling industry in Halifax or to the milling industry all across Canada? The government will have to wrestle with this problem once it grants such a subsidy.
There is also the big danger that if we subsidize the milling industry directly in, say, the Atlantic ports, then the United States, which can and have proven very effectively that they can compete with us-and they are not subsidizing their milling industry directly, although they are assisting it-may well retaliate and start subsidizing their milling industry, thus making if far more difficult for the Canadian milling industry to compete with them.
As we know, 80 per cent of our flour exports go to Cuba. If this bill passes we will be jeopardizing this substantial sale. Maintaining section 272 in the Railway Act and maintaining
Restraint of Government Expenditures the Act at and east rates is the anwer. The section does not need to be changed, and it should not be eliminated. Millers know exactly what their situation is and they know whether or not they will get the subsidy from one year to another. Granting such a subsidy is a dangerous game. This is not the way to encourage capital expenditures. The milling industry cannot afford the risk of a change of mind by the government.
If the competitive position of Canadian flour is reduced by $15 to $20 per ton, the outlook is for an immediate reduction of exports to markets other than Cuba, and the reduction of exports to that market beginning in 1977, not somewhere down the road but in the very near future. It is more than likely that in the longer run Cuba will either expand its milling capacity and reduce imports to minimal levels, or else turn to other suppliers. The resultant loss of export markets will cause tremendous rationalization to take place in the milling industry and require the industry to close several mills.
As I said earlier, back in 1956 there were 78 milling plants in Canada; today there are 39. How much further can we retrench? We have already lost a large percentage of the world's flour market. Ten years ago we captured 18 per cent of it. The flour market has not shrunk, but our share of it has fallen. Today we are capturing less than 10 per cent of it, even with the record shipments to Cuba of 375,000 tons this year. In my opinion it behooves the federal government, in an inflationary period and in a period of high unemployment in regions of Canada where we have consistently had what one might call higher unemployment than acceptable, to do everything it can to maintain the industry instead of allowing it to be destroyed, something which may well happen as a result of the elimination of Section 272 from the Railway Act.
I know that the government will say that it will subsidize the milling industry directly, but the whole purpose of Bill C-19 is to reduce expenditures. If the government is to subsidize the milling industry directly, why do so through Bill C-19, the purpose of which is to reduce expenditures? One can believe that there is no real reduction if one has faith in the government, but one does not have such faith in the government, nor do the millers have it. They have no confidence that the subsidy will be maintained for any length of time.
It can be argued that, if a fixed subsidy is paid, the millers will tend to use the least costly routes. That is an old argument. One would like to think that the least costly routes are being used right now.
By passing this bill on second reading and sending it to committee we can assure the milling industry that a lengthy and careful examination will be given to this aspect of the bill, because we on this side of the House are mighty concerned with every part of Canada. Maritime members are and were violently concerned about the old bill, Bill C-87, and we thought we had successfully convinced the government to delete Clause 15 of the old bill. It was Clause 15 in the old bill, and it is Clause 15 in this bill. We thought that in the last session we had convinced the government to delete this aspect of the legislation. However, the government continues to

November 5, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures plough blindly on, insensitive to the wishes and concerns of the people of the nation, and wonders why it is so unpopular.
The Prime Minister goes across Canada bleating and asking people why they do not like him. People in every region of Canada do not like him because he has demonstrated insensitivity to their concerns. This bill is a prime example of that insensitivity, and so is the repeal of section 272. We thought we had the government convinced that it could not proceed in this manner, but it is obvious we were not successful.
The Russian bargaining agency has told the government that it will cease to buy if flour rates go up. It has told the government that Russia will build a milling industry in Cuba to mill our wheat, the thing we should be asking them not to do. We should be maintaining our industry, particularly in areas where unemployment has been a persistent problem.
The government pays no attention to the wishes of the people, and when that happens it is the responsibility of the people to remove the government at the first opportunity. I am certain that that time will not come too soon for the people who are affected by this bill, and one cannot blame them for feeling that way. The Prime Minister can claim that he is unpopular because he is French and he promotes the French language, if he likes, but that is not the reason at all. He is unpopular because he is insensitive to the wishes and needs of people in every region of Canada.
The government could boost its popularity a great deal if it proceeded step by step, and one of the steps I suggest would be to agree that Clause 15 should be deleted from this bill. It would be simple to accept such an amendment, and the milling industry would be much happier and have more confidence and trust in the government if the government did so.
That is really all I have to say about Bill C-19. I want to assure the milling industry that we on this side of the House will proceed very cautiously to make certain that that industry is not eliminated, that employment opportunities will continue and, if possible, that there will be a substantial expansion. We hope the Canadian Millers' Association will be called before the committee to present its case so that we can ascertain whether the subsidies with which the government will bait the industry will be ample to maintain its existence. If not, we hope the committee will take action to bring this about.
Certainly for me the essence of governing is creating opportunities for Canadians, not diminishing them. This bill appears to limit the milling industry, which once played a very vital part in Canada and which at one time was competitive throughout the world. Now it is not because the European Common Market is heavily subsidizing its milling industry, and we are placing our milling industry in a disadvantageous position.
I see that the Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Goodale) is eagerly taking notes. I hope he has noted my words of caution, because this means a great deal to the grains industry as a whole.

My friend has again highlighted the very inconsistency on the other side about which I was just talking. On the one hand the right hon. member for Prince Albert can be as critical as he was of the Prime Minister and of his visit to Cuba on trading and diplomatic matters earlier this year, and at the same time the hon. member opposite can applaud the trading relations Canada has traditionally enjoyed with Cuba. I suggest that that is a gross inconsistency which neither the right hon. member for Prince Albert nor the hon. member for Crowfoot can explain away as simply as the hon. member has just tried to do. That is an inconsistency which 1 think it is impossible for them to justify.
In any event, in a moment or two I would like to deal with the concern the hon. member for Crowfoot expressed about the milling industry in Canada, but as I begin my remarks I want to deal specifically with another provision in Bill C-19, the one relating to the western grain stabilization plan, which proposes to amend Section 41 of that plan. I think to understand the impact of this clause it is important to understand one or two basic points about the mechanical operation of the western
November 5, 1976

grain stabilization plan. It is a mechanism which is now in place to provide a way whereby the incomes of western grain producers can be cushioned against the jolting, recurring impact of the fluctuations in grain receipts which are so painfully familiar to many of us from western Canada.
The technique adopted is the establishment of a western grain stabilization fund. The fund draws revenue from four sources. First it draws from the producers who will be asked to contribute a certain amount of their gross grain receipts annually to the grain stabilization fund. As has been mentioned, this is a voluntary plan, and producers may exercise the option to withdraw, but if they are in it they will be asked to contribute this levy. Second, the Government of Canada contributes to the fund $2 for every $1 the farmer puts into it. Third, when the fund is in a surplus position the government will pay interest on it. Fourth, the Government of Canada backs the grain stabilization fund with a fundamental guarantee of solvency so that it can never run out of money. It will always have sufficient money to pay out to grain producers on those occasions when payments are required.
The amendment proposed in Bill C-19 in so far as it affects the western grain stabilization plan is concerned, allows possible deferment of government contributions to the plan until that money is needed. When it is needed farmers and people in western Canada can be assured that the full amount will be there, with interest as provided in clause 14. The western farmer's position is protected; there can be no detrimental effect upon the western grain stabilization plan or the interests of western Canadian farmers.
Earlier today my hon. friend opposite asked why the producer is not in a position to defer his contribution to the grain stabilization fund as well. Of course that issue is not as he tries to make out. There are 140,000 or 150,000 participating producers in the plan and, as was discussed thoroughly in the Standing Committee on Agriculture when the bill was before it last year, the possibility of establishing an individual and separate account for each of 140,000 or 150,000 participants would be an administrative nightmare which I do not think even he would want to sanction.
The idea of the levy is that producers' contributions to the fund would be deducted at source by licensed elevators and others. It is administratively convenient and has the sanction, approval, and support of the vast majority of farmers in western Canada and of Canadian farm organizations. My hon. friend opposite will know that some contributions do not lend themselves to automatic deduction at source; they are essentially voluntary and can be contributed at will by producers if they deem it in their interest, on grain receipts that do not lend themselves to an automatic or simple deduction at source.
An important point to remember is that when the farmer contributes to the grain stabilization fund, and when the fund is running a surplus, that money is earning interest paid by the Government of Canada. The money is not sitting idle but is at work for western grain producers.

Another important point that should be highlighted relates to the question that the hon. member for Crowfoot brought up about trust in and support for the western grain stabilization plan. The fact is that about 80 per cent of western grain producers participate, and it has become plain that the number of those who earlier opted out and now want back in, is increasing. It could happen that by the end of the year the participation rate will be higher than 80 per cent.
Any government program of any kind, sponsored by any government anywhere, that has an 80 per cent participation rate-a plan that is essentially voluntary-must enjoy a significant measure of support among the people to whom it is available. In the last few months I have had the privilege of conducting a number of meetings across western Canada and in different parts of the prairies where I have talked to farmers and others about the grain stabilization plan. After more than 50 public meetings it is clear to me that there is keen interest in the plan and a sound understanding of how it is intended to operate. There is a broad measure of support for it. I suggest to the House, with confidence, that this measure of trust and support for the plan is real and is not being eroded by anything taking place at the present time.

speechtext:
Clause 15 of Bill C-19 refers to what is commonly known as the "at and east subsidy" or section 272 of the Railway Act. I think it is clear that this provision in the Railway Act supports what has become an expensive and inefficient system of grain movement which is not in the interests of producers nor in the interests of Canada. It is interesting to examine the kind of grain movement this particular section of the Railway Act tended to foster in the past. If you move grain from the farm to the prairie elevator, out of that elevator into a train which goes from the prairies to Thunder Bay, unload it at the Lakehead into a terminal, clean it, store it for a while, load it on a ship, move it across the lakes-not down the Seaway, but just across the lakes-take it out of the ship and put it into an elevator, take it out of the elevator, load it on to a train and move it further east-if you do all that then you get a subsidy. If you do it any other way you do not get a subsidy. 1 think that demonstrates the problem with this type of provision in the Railway Act. It is a subsidy which is uneconomical and counter-productive, and which does nothing to enhance the system of grain movement we have in Canada.
Bill C-19 proposes that section 272 of the Railway Act be repealed. It has been mentioned earlier today, and it is recognized by this government that such action would have an impact upon the Canadian milling industry. Various ministers of the government have been engaged in intensive discussions with representatives of the milling industry in the last few months in order to try to deal directly with the economic and industrial problems facing millers. The mechanism needed to provide the assistance they claim they require has been under intensive discussion inside government, and outside with industrial representatives. These discussions have borne fruit, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES

Restraint of Government Expenditures Speaker. The minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), will, I understand, be participating later in this debate to explain to members opposite and to the industry the details which have been worked out to provide a more sensible, economic, and effective method of dealing with the problems of the milling industry. 1 think my hon. friend and the industry have the assurance they seek that the kind of proposal forthcoming will meet their requirements.
With these few remarks, Mr. Speaker, 1 should like to conclude. I was interested in the tone of the debate this afternoon, with members of the Conservative party saying that the bill does not do anything, members of the New Democratic Party saying the bill does far too much, and the hon. member for Crowfoot managing to say both of these things at the same time. Perhaps that is rather typical. I hope in the debate which follows, both in the House and in committee, that we can have a full discussion of what is intended by C-19, how it will effectively restrain government expenditures, and have a positive impact upon the economy of the country.
