speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have looked at this so-called restraint act, Bill C-19. Some of the things that it provides do in fact show some restraint on the part of the government. However, I question the effectiveness of some of them.
What first came to my attention was the treatment of the adult occupational training grants. They are set by regulation, not by this House of Commons. The House of Commons will again be unable to approve the appropriateness of those allowances. The minister is instructed to make an annual review of these expenditures. However, there is no suggestion or requirement that he make any kind of a reduction in them. Therefore I am not at all sure what kind of restraint will be shown in that case.
1 notice the elimination of the Company of Young Canadians. I well remember that promise being made by the former leader of this party in at least one if not two election campaigns. While that certainly is a matter of restraint, I note from the Public Accounts recently issued that it will be a saving of something less than $6 million.
I note the removal of Information Canada, another recommendation made by this party on a number of occasions. This will be a saving of $10 million. Presumably some operations of Information Canada will be taken over by the Queen's Printer and some measure of those costs may continue. That is not told to us in the figures that are available.
The freeze on family allowances is a little harder to take. The figure I have heard in the House today is a saving of $230 million a year. I also note a proposal to postpone credits under the Western Grain Stabilization Act. My colleagues from farm areas will adequately deal with that provision as well as the one that proposes to adjust grain freight rates.
I think we can identify something in the order of $250 million a year in restraint specifically in the program. When we are talking of a budget for the country of some $42 billion, an increase of something like 16 per cent over the previous fiscal year, I am not sure that those are restraint measures that deserve very much in the way of laudatory comment.
I want to make some suggestions to the government on some real savings that could be made with restraint. I want to spend a few minutes on the area of Crown corporations. Volume III of the Public Accounts which came into our hands about a month ago lists the financial statements of the Crown corporations. In the table of contents there are no fewer than 43 Crown corporations listed. They run from Air Canada to Uranium Canada Limited. It is not my proposal to deal with all of them, or even with a lot of them today, but I do want to touch on a few, starting at the top with Air Canada.
The Air Canada statement reported an operating loss of $12 million in the fiscal year ended December 31, 1975. That is not a lot of money in the over-all expenditures of the Government of Canada of $42 billion. Compared to the passengers carried it is only about a $1.12 loss for each passenger carried on the

November 5, 1976

airline. However, those figures by themselves hide quite a lot of true financial information.
If you dig deeply into the report of Air Canada you find that the passenger load factor for that year was down to 58 per cent, the lowest since 1971. In a business like that, with huge gross revenues of close to a billion dollars, it is obvious that a very small change in the passenger load factor, which could be achieved through scheduling and so on, could have had a great effect on the expenditures of the Government of Canada.
I should comment that Air Canada does not always lose $12 million. The figure for the year before was somewhat lower. However, there is a lot of money invested in Air Canada. In fact it has a debt of over $1 billion. Of course the government owns approximately three quarters of that debt. In other words, the Government of Canada has a cash investment in the debt of Air Canada of three quarters of a billion dollars. Investment, on anybody's part, might not be too bad provided there is an adequate return. But Air Canada's own report shows that the return on investment is 5.1 per cent-that is an average return; they have had some higher and some lower figures in the past ten years. But we must inquire where the government gets the money to invest at that return of 5.1 per cent.
As we know, the government goes each year to the citizens of Canada to borrow money. If we look at one aspect of this process we see that Canada Savings Bonds probably carry a lower rate of interest than many similar government bonds and we find that the government is borrowing at a rate of something over 9 per cent. And, as we have noted, it is earning 5.1 per cent, which does not appear to be very good business. This makes one wonder what kind of restraint is not being practised by an organization like Air Canada.
I have maintained for a number of years that the government should look closely at selling Air Canada. I understand that when the industry was very young in the thirties, many companies went into business and, like other young companies, ran into financial difficulty. I think there might well have been some justification for the government getting into the operation at that stage, bearing in mind the huge amounts of capital which were needed to get the thing going and the need to consolidate all the companies which were experiencing financial difficulties.
It might be said that the people of Canada could not afford to buy Air Canada. But there is evidence that Canadian investors whether through pension funds, trust companies, banks or whatever, have already invested in bonds covering three quarters of the total debt of that corporation. I was delighted, from one point of view, to read recently that the government is presently considering the return in some measure of Air Canada to private enterprise. I have not seen the details but I am waiting eagerly to see what ideas it has in mind and whether some of mine have filtered down to the government.

speechtext:
Air Canada is only one example of an area where restraint could be exercised at enormous saving to the taxpayer.
We might well take a look at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. We find from an examination of the Public Accounts that for the year ending March 31, 1976, the net cost, otherwise known as the loss, of the CBC in that year was $310 million. This was the figure for the most recent fiscal year; in the preceding fiscal year the loss was $260 million. So instead of there being any kind of restraint program in the CBC the cost increased by $60 million in one year. Even so, one could say, I suppose that that is not very much money because apportioned among the people of Canada it amounts to only $14 per capita. But again we must look at the investment which is required before these losses can be incurred. And we find from the Public Accounts that the total assets of the CBC amount to some $316 million. Bearing in mind then that the investment amounts to slightly more than the loss on the operations this year, it seems that the return on investment amounts to about minus 98 per cent.

speechtext: Not very much.

speechtext:
It is not excess revenue, anyway. They would never get hauled up before the Anti-Inflation Board.
If I can find the report of the Auditor General I have one or two other comments to make on those figures. Referring to the CBC financial statement it says, having set out the figures I have quoted:
The corporation has not recorded accrued interest of $28 million of which $14 million is the interest for the year on loans from Canada and payment of such interest has been deferred until March 31. 1979.
I take it the results were so bad that the people who make up the statement for the CBC could not bear to put in another $28 million of accrued interest. The Auditor General also says that severance pay is recorded in the accounts when paid on employee retirement or separation and, he says,
No provision has been made in the accounts for benefits accruing to employees amounting to $28.7 million at March 31. 1976 and expenses for the year have been understated by $3.4 million.
I suppose this aspect will be considered if and when the accounts of the CBC come before the Public Accounts Committee. However, as hon. members know, that committee is not privileged to examine regularly the affairs of every Crown corporation or even every department, so perhaps we shall

November 5, 1976
Restraint of Government Expenditures have a chance to comment on that observation by the Auditor General, and perhaps not.
It will probably be said that the CBC provides Canadians with some very special features and that it should not be concerned directly with cost. I go along with that to some extent, except that I find that effective the first of this month, for example, after 30 years the CBC has ceased to carry the BBC news direct from London. Now, Mr. Speaker, that is one of the features whose cost could have been included, I would have thought, in the $300 million loss the people of Canada can expect to see continuing.
One of the other things we like to think of, as far as the CBC is concerned, is that we have freedom from most advertising and freedom from a lot of unimportant detail. I find that in place of the BBC news we are to be subjected to sports reports, so we must now listen to what is happening in all the sports arenas around the country.
What is the true cost per capita of this monster of the CBC which is costing us $300 million losses on total assets of $300 million in capital? I do not know what percentage of the people listen to the CBC, but the corporation is obviously competing with hundreds of other stations around the country, so the per capita cost per listener must be astronomical.
Why cannot we get rid of the CBC? We would free up the $300 million we would not have to borrow, and save $300 million in annual losses which we are now carrying. Hon. members may ask: who is going to buy the CBC? Well, I have talked to the radio and telecommunications industry in Canada. These people have enormous resources and enormous investment in their own physical plant. Many of them would take over and pay a fair price for the assets of the CBC.
What would we lose, Mr. Speaker? We would lose a national network to which few people listen. Perhaps in the days when the CBC was first formed it was necessary in a country like Canada to have a national network. But with networks flourishing all over the place-I understand there is not a single independent radio station left in Ottawa; all are members of a network of some kind or other-we could let the CBC become part of another network. Just think of all the resources of Canada that would be saved thereby.
Some might say that no one is going to take radio and television into unprofitable areas such as the far north, where there is insufficient demand for a commercial operation. Well, there is a simple answer to that. If the government would adopt a policy of being a regulatory body, instead of competing with people already in the business, there would be no problem. For example, there is no reason why the government could not sell off the CBC and issue licences as it does to all other broadcasters in Canada. It could make it a condition of the licence-heaven knows, enough conditions are attached to licences issued by the CRTC, the governing body in Canada- that those who acquire the assets of the CBC must serve outlying areas as well as profitable areas.

The advertising-free aspect of the CBC would be lost, but this would be a small price to pay compared with the $300 million investment and a $300 million loss. Perhaps 90 per cent of the people of Canada do not listen to the CBC anyway but choose to listen to some of the other hundreds of stations that operate on a profitable basis with advertising.
Some might say that this has never been done before. 1 see no member of the NDP is listening to my remarks. I did expect some challenge from that quarter; 1 am sorry they are missing out. I guess that is why it is so quiet down there, Mr. Speaker.
Let me give an example. 1 am sure the telephone industry operates well under Bell Canada, but I know better about my own province of British Columbia. The B.C. Telephone Company is privately owned-that is, shareholder owned-a corporation with huge investment from the private sector. All regions of British Columbia have telephone service. How can this company afford to service unprofitable areas and do so willingly? Perhaps it does not do so willingly, but the point is that the government has granted the B.C. Telephone Company a licence-a monopoly if you like-to provide telephone service.
A telephone licence is not like a licence to carry on the road, such as a licensed taxi. It is difficult to have competition in the telephone business because of the physical plant that is required to provide a service. B.C. Telephone Company get a licence that allows them the right to provide telephone service in areas they want to service because they get a return on their investment, but the licence also requires them to provide service in less profitable areas. No government investment is required. No government competition is involved. And people in outlying areas get telephone service at a very reasonable rate.
In fact, Mr. Speaker, I was surprised to learn that in the outlying areas of British Columbia telephone rates are actually lower than they are in the cities. There is a rationale for this. It makes good sense if you stop to think about it. The larger your settlement, the more use is a telephone; therefore the more the company is allowed to require people to pay for its use. The assumption is that the more you use something, whether telephone service or something else, the more you should be willing to pay for it.

Let me see if I can find any area of restraint here. Canadian National Railways is a very complex structure, though it had its beginnings in much
November 5, 1976

the same way as Air Canada. During the twenties there were many railway problems and the CNR was formed to consolidate those problem areas.
According to its report there are 13 separately operated trucking companies owned by Canadian National whose operations are consolidated. In addition to the trucking companies, which of course are competing with privately owned trucking companies, there are 53 consolidated subsidiaries all included in the same financial statement. 1 am not going to bother with the 53 consolidated subsidiaries but it is of interest to note that the CNR never considers that money costs anything. Furthermore, the note goes on to point out that the $91 million loss is before interest charges-here we do know what the total figure is-of $111 million. I suggest $91 million before and after $111 million in interest are two different things. May I call it four o'clock?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
that Bill C-206, to amend the Bank of Canada Act, be read the second time
The Bank of Canada
and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am very proud to pilot this bill whose importance is very significant and I am convinced that if it is passed by Parliament, it will have a very favourable impact on the Canadian economy.
This bill is identical to the one my leader (Mr. Caouette) introduced in the House and spelled out so ably during the last session. The purpose of this bill it to amend the Bank of Canada Act. Although its foundation goes back to 40 years ago, the fact remains that the bank still does not have the authority to make long term loans to the government of Canada or the government of a province.
In fact, paragraph 18(1)(/) reads as follows: The bank may
"(/) make loans or advances for periods not exceeding six months to the Government of Canada or the government of any province on the pledge or hypothecation of readily marketable securities issued or guaranteed by Canada or any province;"
In my opinion, this cannot be considered a way to ease the credit of the nation for financing the public sector to the benefit of the Canadian public.
Paragraph 18(1)(/'), which is no longer valid as it only limited the time allowed for the reimbursement of the advances made, reads as follows:
"(/') make loans lo (he Government of Canada or the government of any province, but such loans outstanding at any one time shall not. in the case of the Government of Canada, exceed one-third of the estimated revenue of such government for its fiscal year, and shall not in the case of any provincial government exceed one-fourth of such government's estimated revenue for its fiscal year; and such loans shall be repaid before the end of the first quarter after the end of the fiscal year of such government;"
In other words, if the fiscal year of a provincial government ends on March 31 and the said government had borrowed $150 million from the Bank of Canada, it will have to reimburse these $150 million not later than June 30, so that the province will find itself financially in the same situation as before obtaining its loan and the vicious circle will start all over again. Yet, the Canadian government is a lot more generous with foreign countries, since it is lending them huge amounts of money, sometimes without interest, and at other times at extremely low interest rates.
Why could we not do for ourselves what we are doing for other countries? The purpose of Bill C-206 is to amend the Bank of Canada Act to permit the Bank to make loans or advances for periods not exceeding sixty years to the Government of Canada or the government of any province based on the real credit of Canada or the province at a rate of interest which does not exceed the cost of administration.
Secondly, paragraph 18 (1) (J) of the said act is repealed. Thus, Mr. Speaker this amendment gives the Government of Canada, through the Bank of Canada, the real power to finance the credit of this nation at a very low cost, which should slow down inflation and enable the government to finance the public sector more economically. The government would cease to be the competitor of free enterprise on the loan market, on the money market.

November 5, 1976
The Bank of Canada
I know that some hon. members are already stating that this will fan inflation. Come on, let's be serious. Whether a $50 million credit be generated by chartered banks and put into circulation through government borrowings for the construction of a public building, or a $50 million credit be generated by the Bank of Canada and put into circulation through government borrowings for the same purpose makes no difference. Would there be greater inflation if those $50 million were generated by the Bank of Canada? I suggest not. Now, there would be a difference for Canadian taxpayers. Instead of paying taxes and levies to pay out 12 and 15 per cent interest rates as is presently the case, they would pay for administrative costs only. We should not forget that a country's monetary system should first of all be a service, not a merchandise which can be produced and destroyed to the liking of those who are controlling it, as is presently the case.
I might be told that those who have money to lend will be the losers, as the rates would surely decrease. To this I would answer that this is precisely the avowed purpose-lower interest rates. But if Canadians pay less income and other taxes to finance the public sector, they will have more income left, which will compensate them for the loss of income issuing from interest on investments. Though there may be more private borrowers than lenders in Canada, I feel that, in the final analysis, this bill will benefit everyone. Here is another advantage of lower interest rates: industrialists, businessmen and the whole private sector would see their operating costs drop, this would lead to a generally lower cost of living, and that is what we are all seeking.
To my mind, it is far more difficult to adopt the metric system in this country than to implement a monetary reform. Still, the government, through an act of Parliament, implements a major economic reform by adopting the metric system. The Canadian Parliament, the supreme authority in this country, has the power to change our monetary system, and one of the best possible means of doing so is to pass Bill C-206.
Mr. Speaker, many people have very confused ideas about money. For instance, they often think money is automatically created by economic activity. That is far from the truth. The beef producer who has a herd of cattle does not create through cattle breeding the monetary value of his herd. I am convinced a large number of producers would now accept those means if it were possible. The production of goods and the production of money are the result of two very different processes:
Money is largely generated through chartered banks, although general control over the money supply is assumed by the Bank of Canada. Under section 72 of the Bank Act, it controls the reserves of chartered banks. These reserves allow chartered banks to create and issue the financial credit used by Canadians but since chartered banks have the power to issue up to 16 times more credit than they have in the form of reserves, these institutions exert a decisive influence on condi-

tions which allow Canadians to acquire their purchasing power.
It goes without saying that credit creation is geared to credit reimbursement with interest. Just as a family can pay a house three times over in interest before enjoying ownership, so do governments usually pay three, four and even five times in interest the original price of public works. Mr. Speaker, there is the cancer of inflation. However, I do not like to make such a statement without backing it with some evidence.
So, Mr. Speaker, allow me to give an example that is quite recent. I refer to Hansard for February 23, 1976, page 11151, question No. 3580 put by the hon. member for Bellechasse and answered by the Minister for Urban Affairs. It is about two housing projects for retired people. Under an agreement between the province of Quebec and the federal government, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation lends the Quebec Housing Corporation 90 per cent of the project's estimated value, and for one of them the loan in the amount of $537,863 at 103/s per cent, is to be repaid over a 50-year period. It is clearly stipulated that the yearly repayment of capital and interests will be $57,61 7.24.
If you multiply the yearly repayment by 50, since the loan is refundable over 50 years, the total amount Quebec will have to pay for these 30 units will be $2,880,862, that is $2,342,999 in interest only, which represents the value of 130 units worth $17,929.00 originally. Thus, 30 housing units for retired people, plus the value of 100 units in interests, which goes to the credit and finance monopoly, that is to say, the loan sharks.
Mr. Speaker, this is a clear illustration of the financing system of the public sector. In order not to be the exclusive boss of the monetary system, the government requires the Canadian people to pay five times the value of a public good, which is why the national debt doubled between 1967 and 1975 and will continue to rise during the next years if we do not have the courage to amend the Bank of Canada Act by allowing it to authorize long term loans to the government with an interest rate equal to the administration costs. If I were authorized under our rules, I would submit to the clerk, Mr. Speaker, tables indicating the difference between those two financing practices in the public sector. The first concerns the fact 1 just mentioned, that is a loan of $537,863 with an interest of l3/* p. 100, calculated twice a year, which means that six months only after the lending transaction, the debt increased by $27,901.64 and that after 12 months, the interest will be calculated on the interest of the first six months, which means that the repayment of capital with the first yearly payment of $57,617.24 will only be $366.56. That is the cancer.
In my opinion, government loans should be made at a simple interest rate, since experts like architects, engineers and other people estimated that the building could last at least 50 years. Thus, it would be normal that the depreciation be deducted from the repayments. Consequently, in this case, the repayment would amount to $10,757.26 a year; thus, the second year, interest costs would be reduced in proportion. It would
November 5, 1976

therefore be on a decreasing scale. The lender could lend to others the $10,757.26 repayment. Even at a simple interest of 103/# per cent, taxpayers would pay $1,423,667.00 in interest, but in any case this would save $1 million on this building. At a simple interest rate, Mr. Speaker, to pay $2,342,999 in interest on a $537,863 loan refundable over a 50-year period, represents all the same a 17 per cent interest rate. If this is not loan sharking, I wonder what loan sharking is. We should keep this in mind when we consider Bill C-16 on criminal interest rate.
This bill gives to the Bank of Canada authority to lend money for financing public utility buildings, for example, a $537,863 loan for the erection of a 30-apartment building, the principal to be paid back, as in the case I referred to, over a 50-year period, at an interest rate of 1.5 per cent, which covers service charges. So, the total cost will amount to $743,150, covering both the principal and the interest, or $14,863 annually instead of $57,617.24. On this particular building, which would be just as solid as the one costing $2,880,862, there would be a saving of $2,137,712. The only difference would be in the financing. The government could therefore build more housing without getting future generations into debts they can never pay back. One needs only look at the increase of the national debt.
In Fortune magazine it has been reported that Prime Minister Trudeau said that the worst complainers were bankers. They take it easy, he said, as never before since I became head of this government. And he added: "I am ashamed. They are making more money than the manufacturing sector or the natural resources sector and all service industries". He is right, Mr. Speaker, when he says that bankers are the worst complainers, but it remains that they are the ones who make all governments in Canada crawl on their knees. I know that some are afraid to attack finance, that some will argue: "Well, if we alter our monetary system, how are we going to trade with other countries?" Let us begin by properly organizing our domestic trade. Are we not free to adopt our own monetary system, as we have adopted our own postal system.
And yet, if there is such a service which does business with every country in the world, it is the postal service. Our letters go all over the world. Whatever the colour, the size or the design on the stamps we affix to envelopes, that comes under an international agreement and it is working very well. Why should things be different if we reformed our monetary system? Why do some suggest that our currency would lose some of its value? It does not get its value from the banks but from our gross national output which comes from Canadians. Money is not the real wealth but only a symbol to measure the value of things and services and also an instrument of exchange.
I ask the Liberals to meditate on the words of the late leader of the Liberal party during a general election in 1935, and I quote:
The Liberal party believes that credit is a public matter which docs not only concern the bankers but which is of direct concern to the ordinary citizen.
The Bank of Canada
The Liberal party is in favour of the immediate creation of a well-constituted national bank to control the issuance of currency to meet public needs. Capital flow should be related to the domestic, social and industrial needs of the Canadian people.
And I think so too. He went on to say:
Once a nation loses control over its currency and its credit, it does not matter much who in that nation makes laws. Once in control, money lenders will ruin any country. As long as control over currency and credit has not been restored-

-its most obvious and most sacred responsibility, any talk of democracy and Parliament supremacy is vain and futile.

Yes, certainly there are other members. 1 am talking to all members, specially to you who think you hold power. After 40 years, do you not agree that it is time to change the Bank of Canada Act to put into practice the ideas put forward by the Liberal chief in 1935?
Since Liberals have the majority, I ask them not to kill this bill but refer it to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, and then definitely passed by the House to give the government a good instrument and allow it to run properly the country without jeopardizing future generations.

November 5, 1976
The Bank of Canada
Mr. Speaker, I think I have clearly explained the scope of the bill of which I am sponsor with concrete examples and tables which I have here and which I would like to be put on record. Unfortunately, our procedure does not allow it. All the same, they are available. Any member who would like to consult them can ask me and I will be glad to put them at their disposal so that they can examine them and criticize them.
In any event, this represents a considerable amount of work and it is well worth looking into by parliamentarians like us who are responsible for running the country properly, so that when we leave this House, we may leave to the next generations something which will make them proud of us. If we leave them in debt up to their neck, they will have to provide for their own needs and pay for our present needs, which is not reasonable. Therefore we must make every effort to control this fantastic increase of the national debt and the best way to do it is to give the Bank of Canada the powers described in the bill.
As for the private sector, it will carry on as it does today, but governments will stop competing with it. The private sector will then be able to survive, individuals will regain confidence in the country and will be able to leave to those following us something to be proud of. Thank you once again for these few extra minutes for which I am very grateful.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert).

I regret very much that I cannot make my whole speech in French. The day I can, I will be the proudest lady, I mean member, in this House. I almost was a female chauvinist.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
I agree with the statement of the hon. member that banks play a sinister role in society today. They are manufacturing credit and making money. Bank buildings all over this country are almost as big as those built by lawyers. The lawyers are also a rather sinister group, those present excluded. They have much to answer for, just as bankers have. If I had time I could talk about frauds and the collusion among the lawyers of this country with which I have some personal experience. I am afraid I must tell the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) that it is happening in his city and that I can document it.
I should like to say a few words about this bill. If this were not a time of necessary restraint-and we have taken so much criticism already from the same people who would support this bill about the manufacturing of money-I might say that the idea might have merit. This idea goes back some years ago to Major C. H. Douglas in the late nineteenth and early twentieth century and some of this Douglas-or Social Credit philosophy-might be worthy of support. I could also say that it would be easy to look at the economy of Alberta, where I grew up, and mistakenly believe something worked because of the wealth today.

1 can remember very clearly the Aberhart period because that was the first contact we had with newspapers. At that time there was what was called "fountain pen" money which was issued very briefly, or funny money. It was a script on which you put stamps. But this did not last long. The economy of Alberta grew and expanded, not because of the money program. Perhaps the old provincial Treasury Branch approach was a useful approach. It consisted of buying and selling your own goods within the province and thus building up the provincial economy. It may have been very useful, but by the same token it was Premier Ernest Manning, and perhaps Premier William Aberhart, who laid the foundations for the strong economy it is-an economy of which Mr. Lougheed now pretends to be the creator and saviour.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: The health of that economy was not his creation but rather God's creation, because it was God who put the riches in the soil.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: And he waited for the right government to come along before it was discovered.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
They have a very good life there; they do not have a sales tax, but it is the richness of the minerals, not the greatness of the mentality of the Conservatives in office at present. Had Manning or Aberhart not abandoned funny money, we might very well not have had the kind of economy that exists there now.
Perhaps in my years of work with crime and courts I have seen too many paperhangers or, in the refined parliamentary parlance of this great House, counterfeiters. They made their money overnight and peddled it wherever it was best to do so. I really do not have too much hope for that system, as much as I admire the hon. member for Bellechasse. I remember the script era. We keep hearing that there is manufacture of too much money, and if money continues to be made this way, it will not be much better or safer than counterfeit. We worry about inflation. Of course this measure would only produce greater inflation, and accelerate the very problem we are now trying to correct. To quote one of the greatest men in this House, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), inflation is a pervasive disease. It causes fear, distrust, and a divisiveness among various segments of society. I do not trust bankers, and bankers do not trust me because I am a woman. We will have to educate Mr. MacLaughlin of the Royal Bank about women in this country.
In the next election we will have to educate everyone so that we can get a few more women in this Chamber. Perhaps then we will not have these superficial banking approaches and resolve the problems with women's intellect working on them-the problems women as homemakers have had to worry about throughout the generations with regard to handling home budgets. It is remarkable that the whole nation is joining in the fight against inflation, and despite what hon. members
November 5, 1976

opposite say, the nation is involved in this-the rank and file trade unionists, the public, and the teachers. We may hear from their leaders who are fundamentally NDP or Maoists- although not all of them-how bad the system is, but they are peddling the Goebbels lie. They figure if they say the lie often enough, people will believe it, but if there was integrity, all of you over there would be-

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Order. Address the Chair.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: The people of Canada want the problem of inflation solved, but they do not want it solved the way you people suggest, with a freeze. You want to freeze everything.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Even through you, Mr. Speaker, it is the same lie. Through you, Sir, I would like to say that they do not know the difference between freeze and formula. The formula for control is quite different from the proposal of hon. members opposite, but they go across the country attacking the very thing the public wants most. They are leaving this House because they cannot stand what I am saying. There are not very many of them over there. There are two Conservatives, one NDP, and three from the party presenting the bill. The Liberals are carrying a quorum. In fact, if you people do not get some people in here in a few minutes we will not have a quorum.

speechtext: Order. Address the Chair.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
I apologize to the Chair, but 1 cannot help but notice all those green people over there. Oh! The green people are really empty seats.
The anti-inflation program we have now has not failed, and I think it would be quite disastrous to try to create more money at a time when the country is trying to cut back. Hon. members opposite attacked and have talked about government spending. They try to give the impression that government spending means we are putting money into the pockets of a few civil servants and into our own pockets. Of course nothing could be further from the truth.
Hon. members opposite should tell the truth because some day they will have to answer for their actions here. The opposition is part of the government, and they may have to tell the truth about what government spending really means-that is cost sharing, welfare, pensions, education, highways, courts, police, prisons, subsidies to stabilize food costs and living costs, family allowances, and all the rest. The hon. member for
The Bank of Canada
Winnipeg North Centre has talked about all these necessities.
I do not know how much he has ever done about them, but they are all necessities of life. Hon. members opposite are misleading the public about the need for restraint, and as much as 1 admire the hon. member for Bellechasse and some of the theories he has expounded here, I must speak in opposition to this bill.
It is dangerous to attempt to mislead the public. The public is already uneasy. Women like me and men who shop know what happened a year ago when we went into the market place and saw that every day a bottle of milk or a loaf of bread cost ten cents more than the day before. Everything seemed to be going up, and we panicked. That is not happening now. In fact prices have stabilized, even dropped in some cases.
Prices are a little higher in British Columbia, but we had an N.P.D. government which bought out bankrupt companies, and now we have to pay for it. Chicken prices, for example, across Canada have dropped except in B.C., but that is because in B.C. the N.P.D. thought it would buy up chicken farms, and sell the birds. Would you believe chickens run by a government? But it was a chicken government.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Had you people shared in telling the truth, you might have served Canada better.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: Order!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, they might have served Canada better had they told the public the truth about the formula. It is not a freeze; it is a formula. It was the contingency plan spoken about long before the election. Hon. members opposite say that the Liberals said one thing before the election and came here and did another. Long before the election the Prime Minister said that there was a contingency plan.
As a reporter before I ever came to this place I remember asking what the contingency plan was. 1 wondered whether it would be a freeze, and at that time I was told that it would not be a freeze; it could be controls. We have controls. The Prime Minister, the former minister of finance, and our current Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) tried to persuade big business, labour, and big government to use restraint. A child who refuses to use restraint requires discipline.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext: So they are children, are they?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED AMENDMENT TO MAKE LONG-TERM LOANS AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION
speechtext:
It was because these interests refused to use self-discipline that the controls were imposed on them. The formula has worked, and I know that makes hon. members opposite very sad. I often wonder whether partisan success is more important than the welfare of our nation.
I think hon. members opposite would have liked the program to fail so that they could have said the government is a failure. However, we have had tremendous success in fighting inflation, and by August of this year the inflation rate had dropped from the 11.1 per cent of last October to 6.7 per cent.

November 5, 1976
The Bank of Canada
The Canadian Labour Congress held a phony so-called protest, which was a fancy word in the 1960's. It was as ridiculous then as it is today. The CLC attempted to attack controls by having a national strike. The CLC did not care about the rank and file trade unionists who wanted to work and to earn their pay that day. It only cared about its big conspiracy with a few leaders of the NDP. The rank and file of the NDP are like the rank and file trade unionists; they have come to me and said that they resented any attempt to stop the rise in inflation in this country, so perhaps at the next election that party will be lucky to have even the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre sitting over there to supervise the House.

However, the program has not failed, and because of that I would hate for us at this time to become involved in anything which inflates the money of this country. I would like to see the controls continue.
The Prime Minister says that controls will be removed only when the inflation rate reaches 4 per cent. I should like controls to remain until we see it go to zero. When prices and wages are set in the post-control period I hope every segment of society will be responsible, and not seek increases as they did in the past. At the present time people are better off than they have been for years. Food baskets are full. Controls have actually improved the earning power of the worker and the value of the dollar; it is more than 3 per cent higher than it was a year ago. Specious attempts to arouse the Canadian public against controls, and mislead them will not win confidence. Indeed we are losing the confidence of the nation by lying to the public. This is an educated public, Mr. Speaker, not an illiterate public. They know the truth. Women comprise 50 per cent of the population, although it does not look like it in this House.

The 51 per cent do most of the buying although today more men are doing the buying and sharing the housekeeping. These people know when members stand here and on public platforms lying about prices, or when the press sets out to create fear in the minds of the public. People who go shopping, who make purchases in the stores, who live under the new anti-inflation controls know that controls are working. They have absolutely no respect for the story that controls should be dropped in Canada. Most Canadians wanted something to be done, and this government responded with its war on inflation. I do not say the formula is perfect, Mr. Speaker. What formula can be perfect that involves human beings? There are so many human variables that there can never be a formula that can resolve the complexities of these variables in a complex economic society.
The Douglas theory was an interesting formula. But formulas do not work for people or for an economy. This formula
[Mrs. Holt.l
was introduced in 1935 and 1 gather 13 acts were passed in 1937 but they were thrown out by the courts and the following year were disallowed. There were repeated attempts to bring the Douglas "A plus B" theorem into the life of Alberta.
As you know, in the Douglas formula, "A" represented wages paid to employees and "B" the cost of production, which was considered essential to supplement A, the wages. B, I presume was $25, I think in script, which could be used at the treasury board. You had to buy Alberta goods. It sounded a good scheme-especially getting $25-but it was dropped. I think they would have dropped it even if it had not been thrown out by the courts. It was not constitutional at that time and 1 doubt if it would be today. Indeed it would be dangerous today to introduce it at a time when we must all work for one Canada and a strong Canada. We must not divide it by a technique of destruction and disincentive.
Again I come back to those who continually tell the lie, hoping that somebody will believe it, and undermine all government attempts to save our tenuous economy, and the buying power of Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, in view of the very deep love the Social Credit Party of Canada has entertained since its inception for the Bank of Canada, 1 am not overly suprised by the remarks made this afternoon by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) on the subject of Bill C-206. According to the information 1 gathered from Hansard over the last few years, similar legislation was examined before. As the hon. member for Bellechasse stated earlier, the debate here was on March 15, 1967. So, even before he came here, there were debates here on the subject of the Bank of Canada. Later on, a similar piece of legislation was introduced on March 18, 1969 by the current leader of the Social Credit Party of Canada, and my hon. friend from Bellechasse referred to it on October 22, 1974. The current leader of the Social Credit Party, the hon. member for Temiscamingue (Mr. Caouette) always showed remarkable conviction during the earlier debate 1 referred to. The sponsor of this bill, the hon. member for Bellechasse, also shows a remarkable sincerity in his comments.
Incidentally, I would like to commend the hon. member for Bellechasse, although I do not share his views, for his persever-ence in attacking not only the Bank of Canada and its powers, by also for addressing himself to a particular subject. In this he deserves commendation. But although I am not an expert in social credit or banking affairs, I believe I can safely state that the provisions included in Bill C-206 by the honourable member for Bellechasse are unrealistic. But the hon. member for Bellechasse, like his predecessors who proposed similar bills, intends effectively to change the role of the Bank of Canada and this could well have some bad effects.
For instance, if you read the first two lines of the bill, you realize that it would change the Bank of Canada Act by raising to a maximum of 60 years the term for loans or advance payments from the Bank of Canada to the government of Canada and provincial governments.
One must admit, Mr. Speaker, and 1 know that my hon. friend from Bellechasse agrees with this, that this would amount to an awful jump from 6 months, as it is now, to 60 years.
This is what I read in the explanatory note on paragraph 18(1)(/):
make loans or advances for period "not exceeding six months" to the Government of Canada or the government of any province on the pledge or hypothecation of readily marketable securities issued or guaranteed by Canada or any province;
